rationale:
Quota today is 1 long video, 3 Shorts and 0 carousels. Everything sits inside the GLP-1 focus.

**Long video (L1): the Foundayo what-to-expect video.** It is #1 on the playbook queue, and the playbook calls this its last attempt with every 11-22 fix applied. It also counts as a search-demand format (a what-to-expect video for an approved drug). Its evidence is settled: the US label plus the Medication Guide. And it feeds our second-strongest engine, search for "foundayo" and "orforglipron": the old video has 536 minutes and the Foundayo Short got 834 views. It was held on 11-22, so it is not live. That makes it a resubmission, not a duplicate, but check the live list before rendering and again before publishing. If it is held again, park it and ship queue #2 (Mounjaro vs Ozempic, SURPASS-2) the same day.

**Shorts: all three are felt moments, on three different body systems.**
- **S1 (hair, 08:00):** an approved drug name plus a visible body moment, Foundayo plus hair shedding. It is a spin-off of L1.
- **S2 (joints, 13:00):** a rising trend. Knee osteoarthritis is crossing into mainstream health news. I gave it a careful, evidence-first angle on an approved drug (semaglutide, STEP 9) rather than on the pipeline drug retatrutide.
- **S3 (stomach, 20:00):** the holiday-table slot, with a new felt moment: vomiting after the big dinner. The holiday angles we've already done (full after 3 bites, heartburn, full the next morning, leftovers, stuffing, bloating, family comments) are all inside the 30-day window.

**What I skipped and why:**
- Hair loss, injection site and pen Shorts for tirzepatide: all covered inside 30 days.
- Cancer and thyroid: news-driven, and covered on 10-31.
- Birth control: covered on 11-05.
- EloraTZP and retatrutide: pipeline drugs, which the Shorts playbook says to avoid.
- Protein and iron: a diet tip with no felt moment.
- Nothing on the radar was marked reject.

pieces.topic: Starting orforglipron (Foundayo), the once-daily GLP-1 pill approved in the US for chronic weight management: what to expect, from the US prescribing information (rev 7/2026) and Medication Guide only. This is the final resubmission of the verified, held script (playbook queue #1). It is not a duplicate: check the live channel list before scripting and again before publishing.
pieces.angle:
The locked label-only script with every 11-22 fix applied, and no new content:
- Regenerate the silent closing scene.
- Remix to masking 0.02 or lower, measured on the final file.
- Redraw the counter-cropped heads and keep the character design consistent.

Keep these locked:

- The label's top dose gave -11.1%. The trial's 36 mg arm (-11.2%) is labelled trial-only.

- The FDA's 'potential' NAION risk, credited to the 9 Nov 2026 Drug Safety Communication unless the live PI prints it.
- 'Your own history of MTC or MEN 2'.

Structure (Exp H):
- Sentence 1 names orforglipron and answers the question with a 'you' moment. No 'Short answer.' label.
- A second concrete payoff at 15–30 s.
- Re-hook every 45–75 s, and land the last new fact before 80%.
- Ending: 'There's a video I'd watch next, linked in the description.' The description ends '…whether it's right for you.'
- Every cut within 0.5 s of its beat on the render.

No dose schedule and no week-by-week timeline. If it's held again, park it and ship queue #2 the same day.

It gives the relief fact as one rounded result: in STEP 9, adults with obesity and knee osteoarthritis had a bigger drop in knee pain on semaglutide than on placebo over 68 weeks. pieces.topic: Threw up after the big holiday dinner on tirzepatide? What the label says about vomiting, fluids and when to call
pieces.angle: Tirzepatide and vomiting after a big meal: the label lists vomiting as a common side effect (rounded top dose vs placebo from Zepbound PI Table 2, with the population on screen). Separate label fact: it slows stomach emptying. Untagged, guilt-free tips: sip fluids little and often unless you've been told to limit fluids, and wait for hunger to come back. Contact your prescriber if you can't keep fluids down or feel dizzy or are passing very little urine, because fluid loss has been linked to kidney problems. Emergency card: severe stomach pain that will not go away, with or without vomiting, means stop using it and call your healthcare provider right away. Then the exact fixed don't-stop line, without 'keep to your usual schedule'. Then the low-blood-sugar line scoped to insulin or a sulfonylurea and adults without type 2 diabetes, 'Not personal advice, so ask your prescriber.' and the loop line.
pieces.working_title: Tirzepatide: Threw Up After the Big Dinner? #shorts
pieces.why: The playbook gives the 20:00 slot to the holiday table through 11-27. 'Still full the morning after' got 513 views. Vomiting after the big meal is a new felt moment we haven't covered in the last 30 days. | fact-check: The label-based angle is fine. The Zepbound Medication Guide pancreatitis line ('stop using and call your healthcare provider right away if you have severe pain in your stomach area that will not go away, with or without vomiting') and the dehydration and kidney warning both fit. Fixes: (1) Drop 'keep to your usual schedule' from the don't-stop line. After a vomiting episode that reads as dosing or schedule advice. Use the fixed line exactly: 'For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop or change your medicine on your own.' (2) Keep the framing guilt-free. The hook must not suggest overeating 'caused' the vomiting or that the viewer did something wrong. (3) Say the gastric-emptying sentence as a label fact, not as the cause of this episode (no 'so', and no 'that's why'). (4) Give the vomiting rate as the label's rounded top-dose vs placebo figure, with the Table 2 population (adults in the label's weight-management trials, as printed) on screen. (5) Add signs of dehydration (dizziness, very little urine) to the 'contact your prescriber' trigger, since you can't keep fluids down. Keep 'unless you've been told to limit fluids'. (6) The low-blood-sugar line must say it's higher with insulin or a sulfonylurea and is also reported in adults without type 2 diabetes.

pieces.topic: Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) vs semaglutide (Ozempic) in type 2 diabetes: the SURPASS-2 randomized head-to-head trial (NEJM 2021; adults with type 2 diabetes on metformin; 40 weeks; open-label; tirzepatide 5, 10 and 15 mg arms vs semaglutide 1 mg). Covers A1C, weight, stomach side effects, low blood sugar and stopping rates, what the trial can and can't tell you, and questions to ask your prescriber.
pieces.angle: Use the same SURPASS-2 deep-dive, but only after confirming no Mounjaro vs Ozempic long video is live. If one is, make this a clearly distinct A1C-focused piece. Suggested title: 'Mounjaro vs Ozempic in Type 2 Diabetes: What the Head-to-Head Trial Found'. Thumbnail: 'WHICH LOWERED A1C MORE?', subtext 'tirzepatide vs semaglutide 1 mg', no answer stated. Sentence 1: 'If you have type 2 diabetes and take metformin: in a 40-week trial that randomly assigned adults to tirzepatide or semaglutide one milligram, A1C fell more on all three tirzepatide doses.' Emergency card: each drug's Medication Guide sentence verbatim ('Stop using [drug] and call your healthcare provider right away if you have severe pain in your stomach area that will not go away…', with that guide's exact clause). Follow it with the fixed line 'For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop or change your medicine on your own.' Low blood sugar: per-arm SURPASS-2 rates. Risk is higher with insulin or a sulfonylurea; the labels also report it in adults without type 2 diabetes. Everything else as planned: open-label and Lilly-funded limits, SURMOUNT-5 as one neutral line about a separate trial, prescriber questions, no dosing, cost or switching talk, and the full 'Not personal advice' and prescriber line.
pieces.working_title: Mounjaro vs Ozempic: Which Lowered A1C More?
pieces.why:
Playbook queue #2 takes the slot now that Foundayo is parked. It's an approved-drug head-to-head against tirzepatide (our best format) with high search demand for 'mounjaro vs ozempic', and it rests on one peer-reviewed RCT plus the labels, so it should pass the fact-check first time. | fact-check: The core topic holds up. I confirmed SURPASS-2 (Frías et al., NEJM 2021;385:503–515): a 40-week, open-label, randomised trial in adults with type 2 diabetes on metformin, with tirzepatide 5, 10 and 15 mg arms (n≈470 each) against semaglutide 1 mg (n=469). A1C change was −2.01, −2.24 and −2.30 points against −1.86. Tirzepatide was noninferior and superior at all three doses. Extra weight loss against semaglutide was −1.9, −3.6 and −5.5 kg. Lilly funded it. Sentence 1 ('A1C fell more on all three tirzepatide arms') is supported. Approve with these changes:
(1) Duplicate risk. The playbook's linking list already routes 'Mounjaro vs Ozempic → Zepbound vs Wegovy', which suggests a Mounjaro vs Ozempic long video already exists. Check the live list before scripting. If one is live, don't re-produce it. Either reframe this as a distinct SURPASS-2 A1C deep-dive with a clearly different title and thumbnail, or drop it.
(2) Emergency wording. 'Stop… and get medical help right away' is the Foundayo guide's wording. The Mounjaro and Ozempic Medication Guides say 'Stop using [drug] and call your healthcare provider right away if you have severe pain in your stomach area (abdomen) that will not go away…'. Copy each guide's own sentence, including its exact 'with or without…' clause. Open each guide and find the sentence before writing it. I couldn't read the Mounjaro guide PDF, and a search summary showed 'nausea or vomiting', which conflicts with the craft note's 'with or without vomiting'.
(3) Don't-stop line. Use the fixed line exactly: 'For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop or change your medicine on your own.' Don't add 'switch' or the plural 'medicines'.
(4) Low blood sugar. Every SURPASS-2 participant had type 2 diabetes. Keep the per-arm rates as printed and the insulin/sulfonylurea line. Attribute 'also reported in adults without type 2 diabetes' to the US labels, not the trial.
(5) Thumbnail. 'WHICH DROPPED MORE?' doesn't name the measure. Use 'WHICH LOWERED A1C MORE?' with 'tirzepatide vs semaglutide 1 mg' as subtext.
(6) Limits chapter. Say the trial tested semaglutide 1 mg only, and say nothing about other doses or rankings. Never call cross-trial numbers head-to-head.
(7) Weight chapter. Frame the figures as trial averages in adults with type 2 diabetes, and keep the paper's measure label: treatment-regimen or efficacy, in plain words.
